item.title: Improvisation No. 30 (Cannons)
item.lesson: Our survey ends where painting lets go of the visible world. Kandinsky — Russian-born, working in Munich with the Blue Rider group — believed color and form could act directly on the soul the way music does, without depicting anything at all; he experienced sounds as colors, and named his most spontaneous canvases 'Improvisations,' like a musician. In this one, painted in 1913 on the very eve of the First World War, viewers immediately spotted the pair of leaning cannons in the lower right corner and read the tilting buildings and smoke as war. Kandinsky pushed back: the cannons had arrived on the canvas unbidden, he wrote — the title was 'selected by me for my own use' and not a description of the picture's contents, which were 'what I was living through at the time... inner desires.' The Chicago lawyer Arthur Jerome Eddy bought it almost immediately — one of America's first collectors to gamble on abstraction — and history granted the painting both readings: pure inner music, and a premonition.
item.lookFor: Find the two cannons at lower right, then deliberately let them go — and notice how the painting keeps organizing itself anyway, through color weight and direction alone. That reorganization in your own eye is the whole argument of abstract art.
